spans.assertion: the analysis used a dataset of 146,028 player-referee dyads from the 2012-2013 season across four European leagues (England, France, Germany, Spain) to study red-card bias by skin tone

after adjusting for position, league, height, weight, and games, dark-skinned players had a 0.217 percentage point higher probability of a red card than light-skinned players (95% CI [-0.001, 0.436], p=0.051)

the hypothesis was concluded NOT SUPPORTED because the CI barely includes zero and p marginally exceeds 0.05, and the evidence is described as inconclusive and highly sensitive to the SE clustering choice
primary risk-difference estimate reported as 0.217pp, 95% CI [-0.001,0.436], two-sided p=0.051
the 0.217pp difference represents an ~17.7% relative increase over the 1.22% baseline rate for light-skinned players, though the CI barely includes zero and p barely exceeds the threshold
secondary estimand: adjusted odds ratio of 1.198, 95% CI [0.999,1.437], p=0.051
odds of a red card are 1.20x higher for dark-skinned players, with the CI just barely including 1.0 (no effect)
the unit of analysis chosen was the player-referee dyad, aggregating all encounters between a given player and referee
found total analytic sample of N=107,606 dyads
found 17,490 dark-skinned dyads (16.3%)
found 90,116 light-skinned dyads (83.7%)
found 1,359 unique players in the sample
found 2,834 unique referees in the sample
found 1,344 red card events, 1.25% of dyads
the model controlled for position, league country, height, weight, and number of games

these five covariates were chosen specifically as plausible confounders linked to both skin tone and red-card risk, each playing a distinct proxy role (exposure/playing style, institutional differences, physicality)
excluded 21,407 dyads (14.7%) lacking profile photos or skin tone ratings
excluded 17,015 medium-skin-tone dyads (11.7%, tone between 0.25 and 0.75) to create clearer contrast groups
final analysis sample retained 107,606 dyads, 73.7% of the original data

spans.note: Transformations heading + skin tone operationalization lead-in

spans.assertion: two independent raters coded skin tone on a 5-point scale from 0.00 to 1.00 in 0.25 increments
found inter-rater correlation of 0.92 and exact agreement of 76.8%
the two raters' scores were averaged into one skin tone score
defined dark skin as average rating ≥0.75 and light skin as average rating ≤0.25
excluded medium-tone dyads (0.25 < average < 0.75) to sharpen the contrast between groups
imputed 46 missing height values (0.04%) with the sample mean
imputed 686 missing weight values (0.6%) with the sample mean
standardized continuous variables to mean 0, SD 1 for comparability of effect sizes
primary specification was logistic regression with robust standard errors clustered at the player level
player-level clustering was chosen as the most conservative approach because each player appears multiple times and skin tone is a player-level characteristic
specified a logistic model of red card probability as a function of dark_skin, position, league, height, weight, and games
marginal effects were computed using the average marginal effects approach

no weighting or fixed effects were applied in the primary model; player FE were rejected as absorbing all skin-tone variation, and referee FE were rejected as requiring too many parameters and risking over-control
the primary result is described as highly sensitive to the choice of clustering
player-clustering (primary) specification: 0.217pp, CI[-0.001,0.436], p=0.051
referee-clustering specification: 0.217pp, CI[0.042,0.393], p=0.015 (significant)
robust SE without clustering: 0.217pp, CI[0.032,0.403], p=0.021 (significant)
continuous skin-tone specification: 0.226pp, CI[0.028,0.425], p=0.026 (significant)
the point estimate is stable at ~0.22pp across all specifications
statistical significance depends entirely on the clustering choice
referee-level clustering yields smaller standard errors and p=0.015
continuous skin tone specification yields p=0.026
England unadjusted difference +0.38pp (dark 1.50% vs light 1.13%)
Germany unadjusted difference +0.67pp (dark 1.47% vs light 0.80%)
France unadjusted difference -0.44pp (dark 1.38% vs light 1.83%)
Spain unadjusted difference -0.42pp (dark 1.20% vs light 1.62%)
the effect appears driven primarily by England and Germany, with reversed patterns in France and Spain
the league differences were not formally tested for a statistical interaction
21,407 dyads (14.7%) were excluded due to missing player photos or skin tone ratings
players without photos differ systematically from those with photos: lower red card rate (1.14% vs 1.25%), fewer games played (2.50 vs 3.02), and much higher unknown-position rate (43% vs 7%)

spans.note: selection into having a photo is non-random; direction of resulting bias is called unclear

spans.assertion: did not control for fouls, yellow cards, or other measures of aggressive play, despite controlling for position and games
the dataset includes country-level referee implicit bias scores, but these were not used in the primary analysis
referee-level bias heterogeneity was not examined
did not control for goals, assists, or other player quality metrics (except indirectly through games played)
did not control for club/team effects

the dark/light cutoffs (≥0.75/≤0.25) are acknowledged as somewhat arbitrary, but the continuous skin-tone measure also shows significance (p=0.026), suggesting the result isn't solely an artifact of the cutoff choice
inter-rater reliability, while high (r=0.92), still had 23% disagreement, introducing measurement error that may attenuate estimates
red cards are rare (1.25% of dyads), making estimates less stable and more sensitive to outliers

the primary p=0.051 result depends on player-level clustering, which may be overly conservative versus game/match-level clustering; referee clustering instead gives p=0.015, suggesting referee-level variation

spans.note: speculates that multiple comparisons/specification searching could inflate the effective Type I error rate

spans.assertion: the dyad-level analysis weights each player-referee pairing equally regardless of number of games played

spans.note: results limited to four leagues/2012-13 season, may not generalize to other periods, countries, levels, or sports

spans.assertion: the independence assumption is assessed as partially met given player-level clustering, with possible unaddressed referee- and game-level correlation
two-way clustering (player × referee) would have been the ideal approach but was not implemented because it was not easily implementable
the no-unmeasured-confounding assumption is assessed as likely violated due to playing style, aggression, and other unobserved confounders
positivity is assessed as partially met: dark-skinned players are underrepresented among goalkeepers (2.1% vs 11.1%) and overrepresented among forwards (35% vs 18%)
did not test for non-linearities or interactions (e.g. skin tone × league, skin tone × position)
the observed heterogeneity by league is said to suggest potential interaction effects
red card measurement is assessed as met (objective, well-documented)
skin tone measurement is assessed as partially met, given high but imperfect inter-rater reliability and subjective categorization
conclusion: the hypothesis is NOT SUPPORTED, with an adjusted risk difference of 0.217pp (95% CI -0.001 to 0.436, p=0.051)
the evidence is characterized as inconclusive rather than clearly supportive or refutatory
the 95% CI barely includes zero (lower bound -0.001)
the p-value marginally exceeds 0.05 (p=0.051)
the effect size, while positive, is very small (0.2pp on a 1.2% baseline)
there is judged to be substantial risk of confounding by playing style and aggression
selection bias from missing photos may bias results, in an unknown direction
the point estimate is positive and consistent (~0.22pp) across all specifications
alternative specifications (referee clustering, robust SE, continuous measure) all show statistical significance (p<0.05)
the relative effect is non-trivial, a 17.7% increase over baseline
the pattern is stronger in England and Germany, where implicit bias may be higher
applied the pre-specified decision rule (α=0.05, two-sided) using the most conservative (player-level) clustering
under that rule the result is not statistically significant (p=0.051), so the null of no difference cannot be rejected at conventional levels

the result is called borderline and highly sensitive to methodological choices, since referee clustering yields a clearly significant result (p=0.015), undermining confidence in any definitive conclusion
even if statistically significant, the magnitude (0.2pp) is small and difficult to interpret causally given potential confounding
the unadjusted difference (0.20pp) is nearly identical to the adjusted difference (0.22pp), suggesting the measured confounders don't explain the association

spans.note: offers two unresolved interpretive possibilities: true causal effect vs. unmeasured confounders explaining the association
states the two alternatives cannot be distinguished without experimental variation or better playing-style/aggression controls

spans.assertion: overall the evidence does not provide strong support for the hypothesis, given the uncertainty and specification sensitivity

further research would need richer playing-behavior controls, game-level analysis, and explicit tests of referee-bias mechanisms (e.g. interactions with referee-country implicit bias scores) — none of which this analysis carried out
the analysis was conducted in Python 3 with pandas, numpy, statsmodels, and scipy, with code (final_analysis.py) and dataset (soccer.csv) provided for reproducibility
no manual data manipulation or undocumented filtering was performed
